## A new memory model: {.smaller .smallcode}

```cpp
template <class T>
struct Node {
    T data;
    Node * next;
    Node(T nD, Node * nN = nullptr) : data(nD), next(nN) { }
};
```

What is the result of each statement?

```cpp
int main() {
    Node<int> nn(5);
    Node<int> * pnn;
}
```

Write code that would result in each of these memory configurations, in order:

::: notes
`Node<int> nn(5);` will not compile on its own -- the constructor takes a
value, so this one is fine, but point out that there is no default
constructor. `Node<int> * pnn;` allocates nothing at all: it is a pointer with
garbage in it, exactly like `int *p;` on Friday.

Then build the two pictures:

- one node holding 8, next is `nullptr`
- two nodes, 6 then 8, the second one's next is `nullptr`

The answers are `new Node<int>(8)` and
`new Node<int>(6, new Node<int>(8))`, and the second one is worth writing out
slowly. The constructor's default argument is what makes it read so neatly.

The diagonal slash means `nullptr`. Establish that notation now -- it is the
whole rest of the term.
:::

```cpp
void insertAtFront(Node * ________ curr, LIT e) {

}
```

Running time?

::: notes
The blank in the signature is the point of the slide: it has to be
`Node *& curr`, a reference to the pointer. Pass the pointer by value and you
change a copy, and the caller's `head` still aims at `dog`.

This is the first place the course needs a pointer to be passed by reference,
and it is exactly the situation the double pointer on PEX2 describes -- a
function that has to change where the caller's pointer aims. `Node **` would
also work; `Node *&` is the C++ way.

Body is two lines: `curr = new Node(e, curr);` or the long form. $\Theta(1)$ --
no traversal, which is the whole appeal of a list.
:::

```cpp
void printReverse(Node * curr) {

}
```

\

Running time? &nbsp; *(our first recurrence)*

::: notes
Recurse first, print after:

```
if (curr == nullptr) return;
printReverse(curr->next);
cout << curr->data;
```

The whole lesson is that swapping those two lines prints forwards. The
recursion is doing the reversing, not any code they wrote.

**Then the recurrence, slowly, because it is the first one.**
$T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(1)$, with $T(0) = \Theta(1)$. Unroll it on the board:
$n$ levels, constant work each, so $\Theta(n)$.

Worth saying out loud that the call stack is holding $n$ frames at the deepest
point -- the space is $\Theta(n)$ too, which an iterative version would not
need. First time space and time come apart.
:::

```cpp
void printReverseOdds(Node * curr) {
    // no items in list


    // one item in list


    // >1 item in list

}
```

Running time?

::: notes
Prints every other node, from the back: for `8 4 2 6 3 1` the odd-indexed
values are 4, 6, 1, so it prints `1 6 4`.

**Three cases, and that is the point of the slide.** A recursion that steps by
*two* needs two base cases, not one:

- `curr == nullptr` -- nothing to do
- `curr->next == nullptr` -- one node left, and it is at an even index, so
  nothing to print either
- otherwise recurse on `curr->next->next`, then print `curr->next->data`

Students who write only the first base case walk off the end of the list on
lists of even length. Let that happen before fixing it.

Running time: $T(n) = T(n-2) + \Theta(1)$, so $n/2$ levels -- still
$\Theta(n)$. Good place to note that halving the *work per level* does not
change the growth rate.
:::

## Example 4: `reverse` {.smaller .smallcode}

<svg class="nodefig" width="520" height="70">
  <g>
    <rect class="cell" x="10"  y="14" width="40" height="40"/><text class="val" x="30"  y="42" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">8</text>
    <rect class="cell" x="110" y="14" width="40" height="40"/><text class="val" x="130" y="42" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">4</text>
    <rect class="cell" x="210" y="14" width="40" height="40"/><text class="val" x="230" y="42" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">2</text>
    <rect class="cell" x="310" y="14" width="40" height="40"/><text class="val" x="330" y="42" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">6</text>
    <rect class="cell" x="410" y="14" width="40" height="40"/><text class="val" x="430" y="42" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">3</text>
  </g>
  <g>
    <path class="wire" d="M50 34 L 100 34"/><polygon points="110,34 98,28 98,40" fill="#1a1a1a"/>
    <path class="wire" d="M150 34 L 200 34"/><polygon points="210,34 198,28 198,40" fill="#1a1a1a"/>
    <path class="wire" d="M250 34 L 300 34"/><polygon points="310,34 298,28 298,40" fill="#1a1a1a"/>
    <path class="wire" d="M350 34 L 400 34"/><polygon points="410,34 398,28 398,40" fill="#1a1a1a"/>
  </g>
</svg>

```cpp
Node * reverse(Node * curr) {
    if (curr != nullptr && _________________) {
        Node * revRest = ______________________



    }
    return ______________;
}
```

Running time?

::: notes
Blanks: `curr->next != nullptr`; `revRest = reverse(curr->next);` then
`curr->next->next = curr;` and `curr->next = nullptr;`; return `revRest`,
or `curr` in the base case.

The move that makes it work: **after the recursive call, `curr->next` still
points at the node that is now the tail of the reversed rest.** So `curr`
already has a handle on where to attach itself. Draw that -- it is the only
hard idea here.

Then `curr->next = nullptr`, because `curr` is about to be the last node.
Forget that line and the list has a cycle, and printing it never terminates.

$T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(n)$, same shape as `printReverse`.

This function returns the new head rather than taking `Node *&`. Worth
contrasting with `insertAtFront` -- two different ways to let a function
change what the caller's pointer aims at.
:::
